paras: The shooting of M. Carter took place early on September 22, 1903, when a posse with bloodhounds hunting a Black man accused of firing on a white man broke into Carter's house two miles from Shelby, Mississippi, and fatally wounded him. Carter was taken to Shelby, and the reports said he would be lynched if he showed signs of recovery.

On Monday, September 21, a Black man fired on M. V. Blum, described as a white citizen of Shelby; one dispatch said he fired "without provocation." The name is printed as Blum, "Vlum" and "Blun" in different papers, and none of them reported whether he was hurt.

A posse took bloodhounds on the trail, and according to the dispatch the dogs led it "straight to the house of M. Carter." When the men knocked, the lights inside went out, and as they broke down the door the occupant fired at them without hitting anyone. The Shelby text said he fired twice, while a Memphis version said he "emptied his pistol." The posse returned fire and fatally wounded Carter, then brought him to Shelby, where the Memphis version placed him in jail.

All three versions said Carter would be lynched if he recovered, the Memphis one adding that he "will undoubtedly be lynched." No later report of his death, of a lynching, of an inquest or of any charge against him was found, and the link between Carter and the shooting of Blum rests on the posse's account of where the dogs led.

The story reached print only as a brief wire item in white papers, every version of it told from the posse's side. The Alexandria Gazette ran a Memphis rewrite on September 23 under "Fired into the House," and the Weekly Corinthian of Corinth, Mississippi, printed the Shelby dispatch of September 22 among its state briefs on September 29. In Arkansas, the Forrest City Times on September 25 and the Van Buren Press on September 26 carried a version datelined September 24 under the headline "MIGHT JUST AS WELL DIE," with the subhead "Negro Wounded and Captured After Firing On a Posse." None of these papers questioned the expected lynching, and the Corinthian's text said Carter's shots had "fortunately" hit no one.
No coverage of the shooting was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Shooting of M. Carter
bases: A posse with bloodhounds hunting a man accused of firing on a white man broke into M. Carter's house and fatally wounded him in an exchange of fire (A1, A2, A4).

A posse shot Carter during a manhunt after, by its own account, he fired on it; the reports call him 'fatally wounded' but none reports his death, and the lynching they predicted if he recovered is not reported to have happened (A1, A2, A4).

Three differently worded versions ran (A1 Memphis, A2/A3 Shelby Sept. 24, A4 Shelby Sept. 22), but they share the same details and phrasing and appear to derive from one Shelby dispatch reflecting the posse's account; no independent or follow-up report was found (A1, A2, A4).

accounts.label: Shelby dispatch (posse's account)
accounts.gist: The bloodhounds led the posse straight to Carter's house; the lights went out, and as the men broke down the door he fired twice, hitting no one, and the posse fatally wounded him.

accounts.label: Memphis rewrite
accounts.gist: Same account, but Carter 'emptied his pistol' and is 'now in jail in Shelby', where he will 'undoubtedly be lynched' if he recovers.

framing.detail: The Forrest City and Van Buren papers ran the wire under 'MIGHT JUST AS WELL DIE' and 'Negro Wounded and Captured After Firing On a Posse', treating the coming lynching as a matter of course.
The Alexandria Gazette's 'Fired into the House' said Carter would 'undoubtedly be lynched' should he recover.
The Weekly Corinthian's brief said Blum was fired on 'without provocation' and that the shots 'fortunately' hit no one.

conflicts.note: Both versions say no one was hit; the Shelby-datelined text (A2, A4) is closer to the source.
A1's Sept. 23 Memphis dateline already reports Carter in jail, consistent with the Sept. 22 date; the Sept. 24 dateline is later filing, not the event date.
Not contradictory; A1 is more specific.
